body:
# Independent audit: conditional ball inequalities and surface repair

Audited source:
`candidate d7f1891e34b3ec5a`.


the ordinary face-disintegration theorem to normal labels. That transfer
is being proved separately and is not supplied by this audit. The entire
source was read; the focus here is its new localization, dimension, and
density-selection mechanism. The surface-measure comparison and contact
domination remain the explicitly cited geometric dependencies.

## 1. Ball cuts and the strict normal region

For L'=L intersect closed B(c,a), a regular boundary point of L' on
the cutting sphere has that sphere's unit outer normal (x-c)/a among
its outer normals. Uniqueness of the regular normal therefore forces
x=c+a v. Such a point belonging to L implies h_L(v)>=v.c+a,
contradicting the strict region V={h_L(v)<v.c+a}. Thus all regular
surface mass of L' over V lies inside the open ball, where L and L'
have the same local boundary. The converse inclusion there is exact.
The singular sets of the two convex bodies are surface-null, proving
the stated normal-measure identity.

The strict inequality in V is essential and is correctly retained.
A positive-measure coincidence between the body's boundary and the
cutting sphere can have equality of support values; it is not being
discarded by a null-boundary presumption. An exposed face meeting the
open ball gives strict inequality in V, and also gives an interior
point of L within the ball, so the truncated body is full dimensional.

## 2. Countable localization and Radon--Nikodym comparison

For every rational ball pair, midpoint inclusion of the closed balls
and M subset K gives (A'+B')/2 subset K'. At a tight original normal
whose endpoint conditional open-ball masses are positive, both endpoint
support faces meet those open balls. The truncated endpoint supports
therefore retain h_A and h_B. A midpoint of those two face points lies
in the middle open ball and has the tight height h_K, so K' retains
h_K as well. All three strict normal regions V apply, and the midpoint
of the truncated bodies is in contact with K' at this normal.

If a rational ball pair produces a lower-dimensional or empty truncated
body, no normal with the just-described positive endpoint masses can
occur for that pair. Such pairs need not be assigned an area-measure
comparison. For every relevant pair all three truncated bodies are
genuine convex bodies, as required by the dependencies.

On the intersection of their open V regions, their area measures are
absolutely continuous with respect to the fixed original reference
lambda, with conditional open-ball masses as densities. Homogeneity
of the power-mean measure inequality permits using this common reference.
Contact domination then supplies the middle conditional mass inequality
on the Borel contact subset. No limit of intersected measures is taken.

There are only countably many rational ball pairs and hence only one
union of exceptional normal null sets. Conditional supports can also
be fixed on a common full-measure set because there are only three
original bodies. The resulting simultaneous rational-ball statement
is therefore valid in the required order of quantifiers.

For arbitrary balls, rational balls strictly inside them can converge
in centers and radii so that each interior point is eventually included
and every point outside is always excluded. Their indicator functions
converge pointwise to the desired OPEN ball indicator, including zero
at its boundary. Dominated convergence gives endpoint mass convergence.
The averaged rational ball remains inside the desired averaged ball,
so its middle mass can be bounded by that fixed middle mass before
taking limits. This proves the all-centers statement on the same
full-measure normal set; it does not choose a new exceptional set for
each center.

## 3. Dimension alignment via Radon differentiation

Fix any x in the support of the positive endpoint law mu_A. Its every
open ball has positive mass. Applying the conditional ball inequality
with equal radii therefore gives

    mu_K(B_epsilon((x+y)/2))
        >=2^(-(d-1)) mu_B(B_epsilon(y))

for every support point y and every epsilon>0. Put T(y)=(x+y)/2 and
nu=T_*mu_B. The exact radius relation is

    nu(B_epsilon(T(y)))=mu_B(B_(2epsilon)(y)).

Absolute continuity and equivalence in the endpoint's affine support
give the ratio of the two endpoint ball masses tending to 2^(-m_B)
at almost every endpoint point with positive finite density. For m_B=0
the ratio is exactly one. The differentiation theorem for finite Radon
measures using Euclidean balls therefore implies

    d(mu_K)_ac/dnu >=2^(-(d-1+m_B))

nu-almost everywhere. In particular mu_K dominates this positive
constant times nu, so nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu_K.

If m_K>m_B, the affine support of nu is H_(m_K)-null, contrary to this
domination and nu's positive mass. Reversing endpoints gives the other
dimension inequality. Actual face inclusion gives
m_K>=dim(L_A+L_B)>=max(m_A,m_B), forcing equal dimensions and one common
direction space. Thus the argument never evaluates a higher-dimensional
target density along a lower-dimensional exceptional midpoint set. The
use of differentiation relative to nu, rather than relative to ambient
Lebesgue measure, is both valid and necessary.

## 4. Pointwise envelope on a product of full endpoint sets

After dimension alignment, the open ambient balls cut ordinary balls
in the common affine tangent coordinates. On each endpoint's Borel
differentiation set E_i, the densities are finite and positive. Because
the conditional ball inequality already holds at all centers and
radii, it can be applied to EVERY x in E_A and y in E_B, even though
that pair is chosen after the normal is fixed.

Divide the equal-radius inequality by omega_m epsilon^m. The power
mean is homogeneous of degree one, so its right side converges to
P_(d-1)(f_A(x),f_B(y)). Taking the upper density at the midpoint gives
the asserted pointwise lower envelope there. The further comparison
with the harmonic-power mean follows already from

    P_(d-1)(a,b)>=sqrt(ab)
      >=[(a^(-1/m)+b^(-1/m))/2]^(-m),

by ordinary arithmetic-geometric means. No target exceptional point
is removed from the possible endpoint product. The upper-density
representative may indeed be infinite at some such points.

## 5. Weighted selection with merely measurable endpoint densities

The compact strongly convex surplus construction needs only compact
marginal supports to produce its locally Lipschitz inverse endpoint
maps; it does not require bounded endpoint densities. For an output
Lebesgue-null set N, its Lipschitz image F_i(N) is null, and

    rho(N)<=gamma_i(F_i(N))=0.

This is the correct absolute-continuity argument. The source's phrase
about 'inverse images of an output null set' should be replaced by
this explicit image calculation, since F_i maps output to endpoint.
It is a wording correction, not a mathematical obstruction.

The weighted area formula then gives h<=f_i(F_i)|det DF_i|. Its weights
may be nonnegative measurable and unbounded. The endpoint marginal
identity ensures F_i belongs to the good differentiation set E_i
rho-almost everywhere. The same positive-semidefinite matrix identity
and trace AM-GM as in the proved density-selection theorem yield the
harmonic-power density bound, and the all-pairs envelope bounds it by
the target upper-density representative.

Output absolute continuity was proved BEFORE removing the target's
Lebesgue-null density-exceptional set. Consequently that set, including
possible infinite upper densities, has zero output mass. The pointwise
bound therefore implies rho<=mu_K as genuine measures. No bound by an
essential supremum, truncation loss, or unjustified evaluation at a
target differentiation point enters the proof.

The couplings satisfying this fixed target domination form a compact
convex set. Every smooth strongly convex surplus optimizer belongs to
it; approximation, finite nonnegative separation, and compact finite
intersection provide one coupling dominating the prescribed old law
for all convex tests. The target measure is fixed and finite throughout.

For m=0 the three faces are points, their midpoint is the middle point,
and the conditional ball inequality bounds the common endpoint mass
by the middle atom. This is a separate discrete argument and uses no
positive-dimensional density formula.

## 6. Scope of the conditional PASS

The result depends essentially on ordinary conditional surface laws
being equivalent to Hausdorff measure on their full relative-interior
exposed faces, with support equal to the closed face. Section 2's
normal-label transfer must be independently justified; this audit does
not substitute an informal smooth Gauss-map argument for that theorem.

Given that dependency, Sections 3-7 require neither a smooth normal
foliation nor a locally bounded conditional density. Measurable assembly
over normals remains the separately audited selector theorem. Preserved
endpoint crossflows and source measures do not themselves imply a new
inequality for arbitrary supporting allocations, as the source states.
No numerical OC payment follows merely from this surface-density repair.
